summary:
Caelum Guard is an early warning system monitoring astronauts’ health daily in space. Its roughly 15-minute routine covers wearable-based heart rate, rhythm and sleep data, urine and blood samples, a symptom questionnaire, a reaction-time test and psychological scales.

Decision-making is layered. Measurements are first validated and erroneous or suspicious values removed. Valid readings are compared with NASA standards and international clinical thresholds, then with the astronaut’s pre-flight values from the same tests; expected space-adaptation effects are not flagged. Combined rules assess several measurements jointly: individually ordinary values may signal risk together. Mild deviations prompt a repeat measurement; serious ones, a comprehensive test.

The psychology module goes beyond questionnaires: when biological signals like heart rate variability, sleep or cortisol deteriorate, it automatically requests the relevant psychological test.

Comprehensive tests match the suspicion, e.g., ultrasound for kidney stones or ECG for arrhythmia. The system issues a preliminary diagnosis with a small, stated margin of error and gives recommendations, but as an autonomous application it refers medication-based treatment to the flight surgeon. Results are packaged for NASA.

Without real sensors or NASA connectivity yet, measurements, Earth baselines and transmission are simulated; once sensors are connected, “Get Data” will return real sensor data.
details:
1. Summary

Caelum Guard is an early warning and decision support system that monitors the health of astronauts on a space mission every day. The astronaut completes a daily routine of at most 15 minutes. The system first validates each measurement, then compares it both with NASA standards and international clinical thresholds and with the personal values the astronaut recorded on the same test on Earth before the flight. Rules that look at several measurements together catch risks that would go unnoticed when each value looks ordinary on its own.

When an anomaly appears, the system requests the relevant in-depth test and, based on the result, produces a preliminary diagnosis together with its margin of error and confidence level. It offers lifestyle and operational recommendations and refers the astronaut to the flight surgeon for any treatment that requires medication. Results are packaged for transmission to NASA mission control.

Because we do not currently have access to real sensors or a NASA link, the measurements, the Earth baseline values and the transmission are simulated. Once sensors are connected, the “Get data” button will fetch real sensor data, and the analysis logic will stay unchanged.

2. The problem we solve: in space, the doctor is far away

When an astronaut in orbit falls ill, there is no doctor on board; support comes from mission control on Earth, and monitoring crew health takes the continuous effort of a large team of specialists. On missions that travel beyond orbit, that support weakens too: communication is delayed or lost, and returning to Earth takes days or even months. Wherever the mission is, the crew must be the first observers of their own health.

Space also changes the human body silently: bone and muscle loss, fluids shifting toward the head, an eye syndrome that affects vision, radiation, disrupted sleep and the psychological burden of isolation. Most of these changes progress without symptoms and are missed for two reasons:

•      General limits do not know the individual. A value can stay within the clinical “normal” range while meaning a serious drop for that particular astronaut. Conversely, normal adaptation to space can trigger unnecessary alarms.

•      Data is scattered. Blood results, sleep records, cabin air and psychological state are monitored separately, yet the real signal often lies in the pattern they form together.

Today, specialist teams on Earth catch these patterns. The farther we travel from Earth, the more this work needs to move to the crew. Caelum Guard was designed to meet that need.

3. How Caelum Guard works

3.1 Daily routine (at most 15 minutes)

The core daily tests take about 6 minutes: syncing the wearable devices, a symptom questionnaire, a sleep diary, a sleepiness scale, a stress slider and a urine sample. Rotating tests are added depending on the day of the week. The wearable, dosimeter and cabin sensors produce data continuously without taking any of the astronaut’s time.

 

3.2 Decision flow

Every measurement follows the same path, and the reason for each step is recorded. Faulty data is filtered out first; a valid measurement is compared first with absolute safety limits and clinical ranges, then with the astronaut’s own Earth values. Combined rules then read several measurements together.

3.3 Four risk levels and stepwise decisions

Each measurement is assigned one of four levels: Normal, Watch, Risk, Critical. Faulty data is additionally marked as Invalid. Decisions are stepwise: a single mild deviation does not trigger an in-depth test; the measurement is repeated first. If the deviation is confirmed or a combined rule fires, an in-depth test is requested.

Eight health areas are monitored: radiation; fluids and cardiovascular; musculoskeletal and metabolism; senses and spine; mind and cognition; sleep and circadian rhythm; immune system; cabin environment. An area’s level is the level of its worst measurement; the overall status is the level of the worst area (Stable / Under watch / At risk / Critical).

3.4 Example case: spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome

The case below is taken from a simulated 30-day ISS mission and shows how the system handles a problem from start to finish.

1.    Day 23: In the weekly vision test, visual acuity is 0.05 logMAR worse than the astronaut’s own Earth value. On its own, this is not an alarm; the level becomes Watch and the test is repeated.

2.    Days 24–25: The symptom questionnaire shows headache and a vision complaint two days in a row.

3.    Day 26: The combined rule reads these findings together and raises a suspicion of spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). The level becomes Risk; the “Required actions” area on the home page requests eye imaging (OCT, fundus and ocular ultrasound) and a repeat vision test.

4.    Day 27: OCT shows a retinal thickness increase of 39 ± 2.3 µm relative to the astronaut’s own value; the diagnostic threshold is 20 µm. The system issues the preliminary diagnosis “SANS — optic disc edema” as confirmed, with medium confidence.

5.    The system gives recommendations (check the cabin CO₂ level, do the vision test every two days), asks for the result to be reported to the flight surgeon today, reminds the astronaut to consult the doctor about medication and prepares the package for transmission to NASA.

4. Benefits and intended impact

Our goal can be summed up in one sentence: to detect a decline in an astronaut’s health before the astronaut feels it, and without waiting for an answer from Earth.

4.1 What does this project change?

•      Problems can be caught early. Kidney stone risk can become visible through rising urine calcium and falling fluid intake before any pain begins; muscle loss can show up as a drop in grip strength before the astronaut feels weak. A problem noticed early can often be solved with fluids, exercise or sleep; a problem noticed late can put the mission at risk.

•      Fewer false alarms. Expected adaptation to space, measurement error, one-off spikes and device reliability are all taken into account; a single mild deviation never triggers an in-depth test.

•      The astronaut knows what to do. The system does not just say “there is a problem”; it shows step by step which test to perform, interprets the result, gives its recommendation and says when to consult a doctor. Whether communication is delayed or lost, the crew is never left in the dark.

•      The doctor receives decisions, not raw data. Instead of scanning hundreds of measurements one by one, the flight surgeon receives a validated, prioritized summary with the reasoning written out, so limited communication time is spent on what matters most.

•      Crew time is protected. Daily health monitoring never exceeds 15 minutes; long tests are requested only when truly needed.

•      Psychological health becomes visible. In long-term isolation, the hardest risk to notice is the mental one, and people often do not voice it themselves. By monitoring the body’s signals, the system suggests the right test at the right time; in the case of self-harm risk, it calls for help directly without making any interpretation.

•      Trust comes from explainability. The reason, source and margin of error behind every alert are visible. In space, no one will trust their life to a system that does not show its reasoning.

•      Autonomy where it matters most. Caelum Guard does not need a live link to Earth to do its job. Validation, comparison, combined rules, in-depth test requests, preliminary diagnosis and recommendations all run on board; mission control receives the result afterwards as a prioritized package, with the communication delay of each location (orbit, Moon, Mars) taken into account.

•      Honest about what it does not know. Every value carries its margin of error and every diagnosis carries a confidence level. When an in-depth test is not reliable enough, the system records the result as “inconclusive” and repeats the test instead of forcing an answer. In space, a confident wrong answer is more dangerous than an honest “not sure yet.”

•      Safe by design. The system never recommends medication and always refers the astronaut to the flight surgeon for any treatment that requires it. For the self-harm item it does not diagnose or interpret; it starts the emergency protocol. Behavioral analysis runs only with explicit consent and only on derived features, and raw audio and video are never stored.

•      Ready for real hardware. The analysis logic is separate from the data source. Replacing the simulated measurements with real wearable, dosimeter and cabin sensor data requires no change to the decision engine, so the same logic that was tested in simulation will run on real data.

•      Open to review and improvement. All thresholds live in a single configuration file with their sources written next to them (NASA-STD-3001, CTCAE v5.0, NOAA, American Diabetes Association), and the thresholds that are team proposals are clearly marked as “proposed thresholds.” Flight surgeons and researchers can review and calibrate them without touching the code.

•      Reliability that can be checked. 62 automated tests cover every disease scenario, healthy data without false alarms, faulty-data filtering, the safety item and the time budget. The same seed always produces the same data, so every scenario can be replayed and verified by anyone.

•      Usable by every crew member. The interface is available in seven languages, shows a written label next to every color level, offers a “reduce motion” option, works on mobile and includes a 19-step guided tour, so no one needs special training to understand what the system is telling them.

4.2 For whom, and when?

•      Today (low Earth orbit): It organizes the crew’s daily health monitoring on space stations and lightens the load on the mission control team. In the fast-growing field of private spaceflight, it offers structured health monitoring to crews who have no full-time medical team with them.

•      Near future (the Moon): It becomes the crew’s first line of decision support during communication outages and when evacuation takes days.

•      Distant future (Mars): On missions where evacuation is impossible and every answer arrives minutes later, it becomes one of the cornerstones of the crew’s medical autonomy.

4.3 Contribution to science and to Earth

•      Personalized medicine in space. Comparing each astronaut with their own Earth values reveals changes that a “same limit for everyone” approach cannot see. The accumulated data builds a person-by-person record of how the human body adapts to space and improves the thresholds of future missions.

•      Isolated settings on Earth. The same approach can be used at Antarctic stations, on submarines and offshore platforms, and in communities hours away from a doctor: a small number of short tests, assessment against the person’s own normal, and further investigation only when needed.

5. What makes the project original

•      Two-criterion assessment: General limits and the astronaut’s own Earth values are used together; expected adaptation to space is not counted as an anomaly.

•      A bridge from body to mind: When biological signals such as heart rate variability, sleep and cortisol deteriorate, the relevant psychological test is requested automatically (Figure 6).

•      Stepwise decisions: Watch, repeat, in-depth test, preliminary diagnosis, referral to the doctor. Each step depends on the previous one being confirmed; the “Required actions” area turns into a diagnosis card as the tests are completed.

•      Tests that can actually be taken, and a system that explains itself: Questionnaires and the reaction test can really be taken in the browser and are scored instantly; the “Analysis Methods” page explains the methods with a live calculator.

•      Statistics borrowed from clinical laboratory medicine. Many alert systems rely on fixed limits alone. Caelum Guard also uses the reference change value (RCV), which asks whether a change is larger than measurement error plus the person’s natural fluctuation. Together with the personal z-score and a biological variation lower bound, this lets the system ignore noise on small percentage values while still catching real drops, such as a fall in lymphocytes.

•      One engine for body and mind. Physical and psychological risks are not handled by separate tools. Eight health areas, 17 combined rules and 16 in-depth tests run in the same decision engine, so a pattern that spans sleep, heart rate variability, cortisol and mood is read as one picture.

•      Confidence is calculated, not assumed. Each diagnosis is scored on four criteria: all triggering data from operational devices, the finding seen in at least two measurements, a reliable in-depth test result, and complete sample information. The score decides whether the result is High, Medium or Low confidence, or whether the system should refuse to diagnose and repeat the test.

•      Escalation that respects the crew’s time. A built-in time budget keeps active daily testing under 15 minutes and sets the priority order: Critical follow-up, Risk follow-up, Watch repeats, then routine tests. Anything that does not fit moves to the next day, and long in-depth tests are requested only when a finding has been confirmed.

•      Built and corrected with real astronaut data. The first version of the decision engine was run on real blood data from the SpaceX Inspiration4 mission in NASA’s open data archive. The trial showed two real weaknesses (false alarms on small percentage values and a missed lymphocyte drop), and the system was redesigned in response. The method was shaped by real data, not only by simulation.

•      Explainable and auditable at every step. The reason for each step in the decision flow is recorded, so every alert can be traced back to its measurement, its threshold, its source and its margin of error. Nothing in the system is a black box.

In one sentence: Caelum Guard does not just display an astronaut’s data; it validates it, compares it with the person’s own normal, reads body and mind together, explains its decision and knows when to say “I am not sure yet.”

6. Detection and decision methods

All thresholds are kept in a single configuration file (config/parametreler.yaml); no numbers are hard-coded. This section summarizes the method; detailed threshold tables are in Appendix A, and the combined rules and in-depth tests are in Appendix B.

6.1 Data validation

Before a measurement is assessed, it goes through these checks:

•      Missing value: treated as “no data”; no level is produced. If a measurement is missing twice in a row, a note is added to the relevant area.

•      Physiological range and unit errors: a value outside the range possible for a human, or more than 100 times the population average, is rejected.

•      Internal consistency: in a complete blood count, if the absolute lymphocyte count differs from “white blood cells × lymphocyte percentage” by more than 15%, the whole sample is marked invalid.

•      Signal quality and sample condition: poor-quality measurements are rejected; if fasting information is required but missing, a Critical result is accepted only after confirmation.

•      Sudden spikes and device reliability: an extreme deviation not supported by any other finding is first treated as a possible device error and a repeat measurement is requested (except for questionnaire answers); a single Critical measurement from a device still in the trial stage awaits confirmation.

6.2 Personal baseline: the astronaut’s Earth values

For each astronaut, measurements are taken 60, 45, 30, 15 and 5 days before flight (at least 3 are required). The mean and standard deviation of these measurements are the astronaut’s “own normal.” If the standard deviation is very small, the within-person biological variation reported in the literature is used as a lower bound to avoid artificial alarms.

Expected adaptation to space is not counted as an anomaly: resting heart rate −3 bpm, systolic blood pressure −5 mmHg, urine calcium/creatinine ratio +30% and height +1.5 cm are gradually added to the baseline over 14 days. For these four measurements, the first 4 measurements after flight day 14 become the new “in-flight baseline.”

6.3 Assessing a single measurement

Each numerical measurement goes through the following steps in order; the worst result applies:

1.    Absolute limits: fixed thresholds from NASA standards and clinical guidelines (Appendix A).

2.    Clinical reference range: a value outside the range is at least Watch.

3.    Personal deviation (z-score): z ≥ 2 is Watch; z ≥ 3 with the value outside the clinical range is Risk; z ≥ 3 with the value inside the clinical range is Watch plus a confirmation measurement. Only deviation in the unfavorable direction counts.

4.    Reference change value (RCV): tests whether the change is larger than measurement error plus the person’s natural fluctuation: RCV = √2 × 1.96 × √(device variation² + within-person variation²).

5.    Confirmation and trend rules: two consecutive Watch results, or 3 measurements moving in the unfavorable direction, are raised to Risk.

6.    Margin of error: every value is shown as “value ± U”, where U = 1.96 × device variation × value. Device variation ranges from 2% to 10% depending on the device type.

6.4 Psychology module

Psychological state is monitored through clinical questionnaires (PHQ-9, GAD-7, PSS-10, BDI-II, BAI, UCLA, MSPSS), a reaction time test (PVT-B), a stress index and behavioral features collected only with explicit consent. Scales without cut-off values are assessed by personal deviation. If the safety item (self-harm) is answered with 1 or higher, the level becomes Critical regardless of the score; the system does not diagnose, it only asks for immediate contact with the flight surgeon.

In the PVT-B, every response of 355 ms or longer counts as a “lapse,” and responses under 100 ms or presses without a stimulus count as “false starts”; a lapse count of ≥ 3 is Watch, ≥ 11 Risk and ≥ 20 Critical. 6.5 Combined rules and in-depth tests

A single unusual value is often not enough. Seventeen combined rules look at values together; for example, “high urine calcium + low urine volume” points to kidney stone risk, and “change in white blood cells + fever” points to infection. In addition, two independent Watch findings in the same area raise that area to Risk. Each rule requests an in-depth test suited to the suspicion (16 in-depth tests; full list in Appendix B).

6.6 Preliminary diagnosis, margin of error and confidence

•      The measurement margin of error is shown next to every in-depth test result.

•      The confidence level scores four criteria: are all triggering data from operational devices, was the finding seen in at least 2 measurements, is the in-depth test’s confidence score ≥ 0.8, and is the sample condition information complete. 4 points is High, 2–3 points Medium, fewer Low.

•      If the in-depth test’s confidence score is below 0.6, no diagnosis is made; the result is recorded as “inconclusive” and the test is repeated.

•      Diagnosis records take one of four statuses: confirmed, suspected, not confirmed (the test came back normal; re-checked after 7 days), inconclusive.

6.7 Recommendations and referral to the doctor

For each finding, the system produces lifestyle and operational recommendations: for example, increasing fluid intake for kidney stone risk, reviewing resistance exercise for muscle loss, and for fatigue, extending the sleep opportunity to at least 8 hours and considering postponing critical operations. Because it is an autonomous application, it does not recommend medication; for any treatment that requires medication, it asks the astronaut to consult the flight surgeon.

6.8 Time budget and transmission to NASA

The astronaut’s active daily testing time never exceeds 15 minutes. If time runs short, the priority order is Critical follow-up, Risk follow-up, Watch repeats and routine tests; any measurement that does not fit is moved to the next day. In-depth tests are outside this budget.

The system prepares a priority data package for mission control with every diagnosis record, whenever an area rises to Risk or Critical, and at the end of each mission day; communication delay is taken into account by location (about 2 seconds in orbit, 1.3 seconds on the way to the Moon, 3–22 minutes on the way to Mars). This part is currently fully simulated.

7. Simulation and testing

Because there are no real sensors, data is created with an astronaut-specific synthetic generator. The generator first produces the baseline measurements on Earth, then the data for the mission days; the simulation is guided by clinical reference values, NASA standards and the physiological changes expected during spaceflight.

•      Four data sets: healthy, problematic, critical emergency and fully random. In the fully random set, most values are healthy; each measurement has a 0.6% chance of a random deviation and a 12% chance of a disease scenario being added.

•      17 disease scenarios: solar particle event, infection, respiratory infection, kidney stone risk, dehydration, muscle loss, eye syndrome, CO₂ buildup, heart rhythm disorder, excessive noise, chronic sleep deprivation, depressive symptoms, anxiety, chronic stress, social isolation, burnout and a psychological safety event.

•      Manual entry and real tests: The day’s measurements can be entered manually. Thirteen tests that require no license or biological sample (PHQ-9, GAD-7, PSS-10, PANAS, UCLA-3, MSPSS, UWES-9, MSQ, MSBS, the sleepiness scale, the stress slider, the sleep diary and a PVT-B that runs on real reaction times in the browser) can actually be taken by the user and are scored instantly. Copyrighted scales and tests requiring biological samples are only simulated.

•      Guided tour: A 19-step tour explains every page; if the user has no data, it proceeds with a temporary sample data set.

7.1 How was the system tested?

•      Trial with real astronaut data: The first version of the decision engine was run on real astronaut blood data from the SpaceX Inspiration4 mission in NASA’s open data archive. The validation step automatically caught a complete blood count record in the data set whose columns had shifted. The trial also revealed two weaknesses in the personal baseline method: false alarms for small percentage values and a missed real drop in lymphocytes. The biological variation lower bound and the reference change value (RCV) were added in response to these findings.

•      62 automated tests: Acceptance scenarios, such as every disease scenario triggering the correct rule and in-depth test, no false alarms on healthy data, filtering of faulty data, the safety item and the time budget, are tested automatically with pytest.

•      Reproducibility: The same seed always produces the same data, so every scenario can be replayed.

8. Factors considered and limitations

8.1 Factors considered

•      Balancing false alarms against missed cases: the confirmation, trend, sudden-spike and linked-finding rules work together to strike this balance.

•      Space physiology and communication delay: expected changes do not trigger alarms; the system is designed to provide decision support independently of mission control.

•      Ethics and privacy: behavioral analysis is performed only with explicit consent and only on derived features; raw audio and video are not stored. Each astronaut sees only their own data.

•      Safety and copyright: for the self-harm item, the system does not diagnose; it starts the emergency protocol. It does not recommend medication. The items of licensed scales are not included in the application.

•      Accessibility: seven languages, written labels alongside the color levels, a “reduce motion” option and a mobile view.

•      Transparency: the application is not a medical device but a decision support tool; thresholds that are proposals are clearly marked as “proposed thresholds.”

8.2 Limitations and next steps

•      The data is simulated. Because there are no real sensors and no astronaut available to try the system, the data is simulated. The next stage is connecting real sensors; once wearable devices and portable analyzers are connected, the analysis logic will work with real data without change.

•      Proposed thresholds: For some thresholds, no space-specific source exists in the literature, so team proposals were used and should be calibrated with data: 50 mSv for solar particle event dose, the weights and thresholds of the stress index, the stress slider thresholds, the biological trigger thresholds, PSQI ≥ 11, a cortisol ratio of 0.35, 80% exercise adherence, a 2-hour mid-sleep shift and the device variation coefficients.

•      Diagnostic accuracy: Sensitivity and specificity values for the in-depth tests have not yet been entered.

•      Who performs the tests: In space, the astronaut takes the questionnaires and daily tests themselves; in-depth tests such as OCT and ultrasound are performed by the astronaut or the crew medical officer.

•      Scales and translations: Which versions of the MSQ and MSBS will be used still needs to be clarified. Languages other than Turkish and English are machine-translated; questionnaire items have not been checked against official translations.

Our long-term goal is that no astronaut, however far from Earth, should ever have to make a decision about their health alone and uninformed.

9. Tools, languages, hardware and software used

•      Analysis engine: Python (3.11 or later), pydantic (data models), NumPy and pandas (computation), PyYAML (threshold catalog).

•      Server: FastAPI and Uvicorn; sessions are kept in cookies and passwords are stored as salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hashes (200,000 iterations).

•      Interface: HTML5, CSS and framework-free JavaScript; Plotly for charts. Seven languages (English, Russian, Japanese, German, French, Italian, Turkish), desktop and mobile views.

•      Testing: 62 automated tests with pytest.

•      Hardware: No hardware was used at this stage. The design targets device types available on a space station, such as wearables, a portable blood analyzer, a blood count analyzer, a dosimeter, cabin CO₂ and noise sensors, ultrasound, OCT and ECG.

•      Sources: NASA-STD-3001 (radiation and CO₂ limits), the NOAA solar radiation storm scale, CTCAE v5.0, American Diabetes Association hypoglycemia levels, Basner et al. 2011 (PVT-B), Van Dongen et al. 2003 (chronic sleep restriction), Kroenke and Spitzer (PHQ-9 and GAD-7), Fraser (reference change value), NASA open data archive (SpaceX Inspiration4).

10. Use of artificial intelligence

The core idea of the project, the testing process, the health areas to be monitored, the scope of the psychology module and the interface requirements belong to the team. We used artificial intelligence (Claude, Anthropic) for:

•      reviewing NASA data sets,

•      coding,

•      editing and translating texts.

Every method and threshold proposed by the AI was reviewed and approved by the team.
